title: Two Years of Organoid Electrophysiology — SUSTech Open Meeting
excerpt: From rigid MEA to MESH-GRIP: the road to better electrophysiology monitoring on organoids, across three generations of mesh liquid metal-polymer conductor interfaces.
body: How do we record meaningful electrophysiological signals from miniature brains in a dish — tissues that reshape themselves over days, that wrinkle and swell and migrate? That question guided the narrative of my SUSTech Open Meeting presentation, and it's the thread that has run through the past two years of my research.

The title was "Road to Better Electrophysiology Monitoring on Organoid: Evolution of Mesh Liquid Metal-Polymer Conductor Based Interfaces" — a mouthful, but the idea is simple: build an electrode interface that moves with the organoid, not against it.
Why Organoid Electrophysiology Matters

Organoids have emerged as one of the most powerful in vitro models available. They capture aspects of developmental biology that monolayer cultures cannot, and they offer a window into disease mechanisms and translational medicine that animal models sometimes obscure. But the real frontier is electrophysiology — reading the electrical language of these miniature organs as they mature and respond to stimuli.

As early as 2022, Cortical Lab reported a landmark demonstration: human brain neurons cultured on a multielectrode array (MEA) learned to play Pong. The system — called DishBrain — showed that in vitro neural tissues could form adaptive, goal-directed behaviour. Shortly after, Cai's Lab developed Brainoware, using brain organoids on MEA chips to perform voice classification. These weren't just stunts; they proved that the combination of organoids and electrophysiology could narrow the gap between science fiction and reality.

The Catch
Both DishBrain and Brainoware used traditional silicon-based planar MEAs. And that's the problem — planar MEAs were never designed for three-dimensional, mechanically dynamic tissues like organoids.
Three Problems with Planar MEA
The limitations of traditional silicon-based MEAs fall into three categories:
<ol>

• Conformity failure: A rigid, flat interface cannot conform to the rugged, ever-changing surface of an organoid. The result is a low channel activation rate — most electrodes aren't touching anything useful.
• Contact instability: Even when contact is made, it's fragile. Fluid movement in the culture medium, or the organoid's own migration, can break the connection at any moment.
• Spatial blindness: A planar MEA only interrogates the bottom surface of a 3D tissue. The sides and top — most of the organoid — are electrophysiologically invisible.

Researchers in top labs around the world have turned their attention to flexible electronic interfaces to address these issues. The general strategies include: 3D needle-like structures for invasive interrogation, mesh architectures for conformal attachment, sandwich configurations for dual-surface coverage, and scaffold- or thread-assisted insertion methods.
Evolution of the Interface

The foundation of my work began with Dr. Wu Yan's Mesh Liquid Metal Polymer Conductor (Mesh MPC), fabricated via microfluidic patterning. This interface uses a TPU mesh as the substrate — soft, stretchable, and capable of conforming to curved organoid surfaces. Two pieces of Mesh MPC can cross and overlap to form a sandwich structure, enveloping the organoid from both sides. That design became the cornerstone of everything that followed, and the starting point of my research journey.
Generation 1 — Mesh MPC (Mild Contact)

The first-generation interface adopted a gentle contact strategy. The mesh draped over the organoid without penetrating or compressing it — biocompatible, but with a trade-off. Because there remained a slight gap between the electrode and the tissue surface, achieving robust signal coupling required waiting for cell proliferation and migration to fill the void. This could take days.
For long-term studies, this is acceptable. For faster experiments, it's a bottleneck.
Generation 2 — MESH-GRIP (Microneedle Integration)

To solve the coupling delay, we designed a second-generation interface that introduces microneedles into the mesh. The needles penetrate slightly into the tissue, establishing immediate electrical contact and forming a mechanically more stable connection. The mesh itself was also made thinner, improving conformability further.
The fabrication process involved several innovations:
<ul>
• 3D-printed resin moulds replace traditional silicon wafers for building the needle structures — faster, cheaper, and easily iterable
• Graphene paste fills the microneedle pores via vacuum negative pressure, creating hardened conductive tips that resist leakage (liquid metal needles, by contrast, leak when poked)

• Sodium alginate encapsulation: a protective coat is applied, and PDMS completes the encapsulation through spontaneous infiltration — a clean, selective method that leaves the microneedle tips exposed

Why Graphene Needles
Graphene forms a harder structure than liquid metal and eliminates leakage risk under mechanical stress. When we poked both types with tweezers, the liquid metal needles leaked while the graphene needles held. Critically, introducing graphene did not degrade electrode conductivity — impedance data confirmed comparable performance. For biosecurity in long-term culture, graphene microneedles are the safer choice.

Characterisation backed up the design. Impedance testing showed good conductivity and batch-to-batch consistency. Stretch cycling revealed a surprising finding — stretching slightly enhanced electrode performance, likely due to favourable reorganisation of the conductive filler network. Accelerated aging tests showed no serious degradation.

The most important number: channel activation rate. Traditional 2D MEAs achieve less than 50%. MESH-GRIP maintains over 60% — a significant improvement that translates directly to richer electrophysiological datasets.
Generation 3 — Foldable Belt (In Progress)

We haven't stopped at microneedles. The third-generation interface introduces a fundamentally different architecture: a foldable belt structure that forms a sandwich configuration from a single piece of MPC, eliminating the alignment complexity of two separate mesh pieces.
Key developments so far:
<ul>
• The folding section is an adjustable belt with electrodes distributed along its length for multi-site organoid monitoring
• Integration with Transwell inserts — the mesh replaces the insert's semipermeable membrane, making the interface compatible with standard cell culture workflows

• Electrical connectivity: we tested aluminium and copper contact points. Copper showed more stable impedance but developed rust over time — a fatal flaw that contaminates the culture well. We switched to SEM conductive carbon tape, which avoids corrosion entirely
• Pogo pins complete the circuit path from MPC to external readout, and full-circuit testing (excluding PCB) confirmed the system works end-to-end
Presentation Takeaways

Preparing this talk forced a clarity that benefits everything downstream. Explaining the evolution from rigid to flexible to stretchable — and articulating why conformity beats conductivity as the primary design constraint — sharpened how we frame the problem in paper drafts and discussions with collaborators.
If you can't explain it to a first-year graduate student, you don't understand it well enough.

Faculty feedback was particularly valuable on two points: (1) how to explain flexible bioelectronics to a general technical audience without losing the physics, and (2) the importance of framing the organoid-interface relationship as a mechanical problem first, with electrical performance following naturally from good contact.
Where We Go Next
Three priorities for the coming months:
<ol>
• Fabricate more third-generation MPCs for device integration and systematic testing
• Explore new methods to build reliable contact points between pogo pins and the MPC interface
• Validate the Transwell-MPC platform with long-term organoid culture and electrophysiological recording
